title: Checkpoint: Your Place in the Universe
objective: After this level you can trace Earth's address from our planet all the way out to the observable universe.
summary: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, Andromeda is ~2.5 million light-years away, and the observable universe holds billions of galaxies in a ~13.8-billion-year-old cosmos.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale. Let's zoom all the way out.
cards.body: Remember the cosmic mailing address from Level 1? Earth, the solar system, the Milky Way. Time to find out how big that last line is, and what lies beyond it.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is a distance, so light leaving one edge would take about 100,000 years to reach the other. In Level 8, Proxima Centauri at 4.2 light-years felt far. Our galaxy is more than 20,000 times wider than that. The suburbs are big.

cards.fact: Andromeda, the nearest large spiral galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
cards.context: You could line up 25 Milky Ways in that gap. Yet on a dark night you can see Andromeda with the naked eye, as a faint smudge. That smudge is a whole galaxy, and the light reaching your eye took about 2.5 million years to get here.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: Andromeda is just one galaxy. The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, many with billions of stars each. And the universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times the Sun's age. So here's the full address: one planet, around one star, in one galaxy among billions.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across
Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away
The observable universe holds billions of galaxies
The universe is about 13.8 billion years old

questions.prompt: About how old is the universe?

options.label: 100,000 years
options.rationale: Far too young: the Sun alone is billions of years old.

options.label: 4.6 billion years
options.rationale: That's the age of the Sun.

questions.explanation: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times older than the Sun.

questions.prompt: From Level 8: Andromeda is 2.5 million light-years away. What does that mean?

options.label: It takes 2.5 million years to fly there
options.rationale: No spacecraft goes anywhere near light speed.

options.label: It’s 2.5 million kilometers from Earth
options.rationale: A light-year is vastly longer than a kilometer.

options.label: The galaxy itself is 2.5 million years old
Its light took 2.5 million years to reach us

questions.explanation: A light-year is a distance; Andromeda's light has been traveling for about 2.5 million years.

questions.prompt: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Roughly how long would light take to cross it?

options.label: About 100,000 seconds
options.rationale: A light-year is a year of light travel, not a second.

options.label: About 13.8 billion years
options.rationale: That's the age of the universe.

questions.explanation: A distance of 100,000 light-years takes light 100,000 years to cross. That's our own galaxy.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: which galaxy is the Sun part of?

options.label: Andromeda
options.rationale: Andromeda is our neighbor, not our home.

options.label: The Large Magellanic Cloud
options.rationale: That's a small satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

options.label: The solar system
options.rationale: The solar system is inside a galaxy, not a galaxy itself.

questions.explanation: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way.

questions.prompt: Chapter 1 recap: which of these is farthest from Earth?

options.label: Proxima Centauri
options.rationale: About 4.2 light-years: the nearest star after the Sun.

options.label: Neptune
options.rationale: The farthest planet, but still inside our solar system.

questions.explanation: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, far beyond every star in our own galaxy.
